4. Risks: a crowded market, thin margins, and operator reliability.
5. Recommendation: test the bundle in a few routes with strong operator partners.
6. Metrics: bundle attach rate, margin per booking, and repeat use.

Twitch exclusive contracts.hint: Exclusive deals buy attention, but they can cost more than they bring back. Measure the return on each deal.
Twitch exclusive contracts.solution:
1. Value: a top streamer can attract viewers and subscribers who stay on the platform.
2. Cost: multi-million deals must be recovered through subscriptions, ads, and creator loyalty.
3. Measure: viewers gained, subscription growth, and retention of the streamer's audience after the contract.
4. Alternatives: revenue-share deals that link payments to performance.
5. Recommendation: use exclusives selectively, with clear milestones and performance-based pay.
6. Metrics: return on deal spend, retention of viewers after the deal, and subscriber growth.

UrbanCompany beauty services.hint: Working professionals want predictable, quick services at home. A subscription should remove the need to book each time.
UrbanCompany beauty services.solution:
1. Users: working professionals in cities who want regular grooming without taking time off.
2. Packages: monthly plans with a fixed set of services and preferred time slots.
3. Convenience: one-tap rebooking and reminders before each visit.
4. Quality: the same trained professional where possible.
5. Pricing: a monthly fee that is cheaper than booking each service.
6. Metrics: subscriber retention, visits per month, and satisfaction.

Bumble BFF expansion.hint: BFF users pay less than dating users. Find features that are worth paying for, like group events or premium friend matching, without locking basic friendship.
Bumble BFF expansion.solution:
1. Users: people who want new friends, often in a new city.
2. Monetisation: paid events and group activities, a premium matching filter, and a 'friend ready' badge.
3. Keep the core free: basic matching and chat should stay free to build the network.
4. Test: premium events in a few cities and watch attendance and repeat use.
5. Risk: a paywall can block the friend network that makes the product work.
6. Metrics: paying users, event attendance, and friends formed per user.

0-0.intro: This week builds the PM basics: how to think about users and jobs before features.
keyIdeas: A job-to-be-done is the progress a user is trying to make, not the feature they asked for.
Strong product cases start with the user and the problem, then options, then a recommendation.
Write your own JTBD analysis for a real app you use; the interviewer will ask why, not just what.
0-0.doneWhen: You can explain JTBD in two sentences and write one structured product case without help.

0-1.intro: Metrics tell you if a product is working. This week you learn to pick one that matters.
keyIdeas: A North Star metric captures the core value users get; OMTM is the one metric the team focuses on this month.
Input metrics are what you control; output metrics are the results you care about.
A one-pager ties a user problem to a flow and a metric. Keep it to one page.
0-1.doneWhen: You can name a North Star for a product and justify it with an input metric and an output metric.

0-2.intro: Get enough AI literacy to talk to engineers and to judge what an AI feature can and cannot do.
keyIdeas: Tokens, context windows and inference cost decide what a feature can afford.
Supervised learning learns from labelled examples; embeddings turn text into vectors so similar things sit close together.
Use an AI tool daily for five different tasks and note where it fails.
0-2.doneWhen: You can explain tokens, context windows, and embeddings to a non-technical friend in plain language.

0-3.intro: Data and retrieval skills let you check your product's numbers and build a simple AI prototype.
keyIdeas: JOINs combine tables, GROUP BY summarises, window functions compare rows, and CTEs break queries into steps.
RAG works in four steps: embed documents, store them, retrieve the closest ones, then generate an answer grounded in them.
A small RAG prototype teaches you more about failure modes than reading about them.
0-3.doneWhen: Your 10 SQL queries run correctly and your RAG prototype answers questions from your own documents.

1-0.intro: Analysis and specs: this week you turn data questions and product ideas into a clear PRD.
keyIdeas: Cohort queries show whether users stick around; compare cohorts, not just totals.
A PRD for an AI feature needs the problem, users, success metrics, and the failure cases.
Competitor features show what users already accept; study three before you propose yours.
1-0.doneWhen: Your analytics notebook answers a real question and your PRD lists success metrics and failure cases.

1-1.intro: Experiments and prompts: test product changes properly, and get reliable output from language models.
keyIdeas: An A/B test needs a hypothesis, a sample size set in advance, and guardrail metrics that must not get worse.
Prompts work better with a clear role, the task, the context, and the output format.
A prompt library lets you reuse what works for common PM tasks.
1-1.doneWhen: You can design an A/B test with a sample size and guardrails, and your prompt library works on five tasks.

1-2.intro: Start the flagship project: a working AI product you can show, built from a real user problem.
keyIdeas: Define the user and problem before you choose the stack.
An MVP can be a simple app with one model call; the value is in the system prompt and the testing.
Test with real examples, including messy ones, and record what changed each iteration.
1-2.doneWhen: You have a working prototype and a log of five test cases with what you changed after each.

1-3.intro: Evaluation is how you know an AI product is good. This week you build a way to measure it.
keyIdeas: Deterministic checks catch format errors; LLM-as-judge scores quality, but check the judge against human scores.
Observability tools record each model call, cost and latency so you can debug real usage.
Hallucinations and bias need specific tests, not general worry.
1-3.doneWhen: Your eval pipeline runs automatically, scores the flagship, and your case study has real numbers.

2-0.intro: Go deeper on retrieval: a domain assistant shows whether you can make RAG work on hard material.
keyIdeas: Chunk size and overlap change what the retriever can find; test them, do not guess.
Hybrid search combines keyword and vector matches and often beats either alone.
Metadata filters stop the model answering from the wrong document.
2-0.doneWhen: Your domain assistant returns sources for its answers, and your notes compare two chunking strategies.

2-1.intro: Ship it. A product with real users teaches more than any amount of practice.
keyIdeas: Deploying to a public URL is part of the product, so treat it as a launch.
Structured feedback (a thumbs-up with a reason) gives you usable data.
Iterate on the top two complaints before adding features.
2-1.doneWhen: Your flagship is live, ten people have used it, and you have changed it based on their feedback.

2-2.intro: Advanced prompting and evaluation: learn the tools that make AI output reliable in production.
keyIdeas: Function calling and structured outputs turn free text into data your product can use.
Compare models on the same eval set; the cheapest model is often good enough for simple steps.
Cost and latency per request decide whether a feature is viable at scale.
2-2.doneWhen: You have a rubric, a model comparison table, and a cost-per-task number for your flagship.

2-3.intro: Turn your work into a portfolio that a hiring manager can scan in two minutes.
keyIdeas: Lead with the problem and the measured impact, not the tech stack.
A two-minute demo shows the product working; record it once, keep it short.
A clean README explains what the product does, how to run it, and what you learned.
2-3.doneWhen: Your case study has a number for impact, your demo is under two minutes, and your repo is clean.

3-0.intro: Agents chain steps together. Learn when that is worth the complexity and when it is not.
keyIdeas: An agent is a model that picks tools and steps; each extra step adds cost and failure.
Graphs make the steps and branches explicit, so you can test each one.
Document what the agent cannot do yet, as clearly as what it can.
3-0.doneWhen: Your agent completes a two-step task and your architecture note explains each step and its failure mode.

3-1.intro: Multimodal products (images, audio, video) bring new costs and new failure modes.
keyIdeas: Diffusion models generate images by refining noise; video is costly because each frame adds work.
Vision and audio APIs cost more per request than text; estimate per-task cost before you design.
Multimodal features need clear fallbacks when the input is poor (blur, noise, accents).
3-1.doneWhen: Your multimodal prototype works on good input, falls back gracefully on bad input, and has a cost estimate.

3-2.intro: Safety is part of the product. Design guardrails before a user finds the gap.
keyIdeas: PII (personal data) must be detected and handled before it reaches a model or a log.
Jailbreaks try to make a model ignore its rules; test with adversarial inputs.
Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews the decisions the model is unsure about.
3-2.doneWhen: Your guardrail blocks the test cases you wrote, and your HITL flow names who reviews what.

3-3.intro: Build in public: sharing real data about your work builds trust and gets you noticed.
keyIdeas: Show trade-offs with numbers: cost, latency and quality, not only screenshots.
Write for the reader who is learning what you learned.
Engagement comes from specific claims that others can check.
3-3.doneWhen: You have published two or three posts, each with a real number from your project.

4-0.intro: Your resume is a filter. Make it easy for both software and a recruiter to read.
keyIdeas: Use a plain, reverse-chronological layout; avoid tables and graphics that parsers misread.
Each bullet is action, tool, and outcome with a number.
A reviewer who is a PM will catch what you miss.
4-0.doneWhen: Every bullet has an outcome with a number, and one PM or mentor has reviewed it.

4-1.intro: Your LinkedIn is the second resume. Make it match the story your resume tells.
keyIdeas: A headline that names the role you want and one proof point works better than a job title.
Feature your portfolio links so a visitor sees the work first.
Use the keywords recruiters search for, in the About section and the skills list.
4-1.doneWhen: Your headline, Featured section and About section all tell the same story as your resume.

4-2.intro: Product sense interviews test how you think under constraints. Practice out loud.
keyIdeas: Structure matters more than the answer: clarify, options, trade-offs, recommendation.
A constraint curveball (a budget cut, a regulation) tests whether your plan still holds.
Record one mock and listen back for filler and unclear steps.
4-2.doneWhen: You have done five mocks and can handle a constraint change without restarting your answer.

4-3.intro: Guesstimates and behavioural stories are where many candidates lose points. Practise both.
keyIdeas: Say your assumptions out loud and sanity-check the final number against something you know.
Behavioural answers use STAR: situation, task, action, result; spend most time on your action.
Anchor each story in a project you can talk about in depth.
4-3.doneWhen: You have four to six STAR stories and five guesstimates with written structures.

5-0.intro: Enterprise AI is where many jobs are. Learn what businesses buy and why.
keyIdeas: Enterprise buyers care about data access, security, and measurable return.
Personalisation and recommender systems are a common product area; know the basics.
Good conversations at meetups lead to referrals; prepare two questions for each.
5-0.doneWhen: You can explain your enterprise agent design to a non-engineer and got feedback from one person in the field.

5-1.intro: Prioritise AI opportunities with a framework, then reach out with a specific reason.
keyIdeas: Score opportunities on value, feasibility, and risk, and say what would change your ranking.
Synthetic data helps when real data is scarce or sensitive; know its limits.
Outreach works when it names something specific the company did.
5-1.doneWhen: You have a ranked list of ten target companies and a short, specific outreach message for each.

5-2.intro: This is the application push. Quality per application matters more than volume.
keyIdeas: Tailor the first two lines of each application to the role.
Referrals are faster than cold applications; ask for them in person or by message.
Keep solving two or three cases a week so your skill does not drop during the search.
5-2.doneWhen: You have sent the target number of applications, and your referral conversations are logged.

5-3.intro: Final push: small improvements and steady practice. Do not start new projects now.
keyIdeas: Check your totals against the plan: applications, referrals, cases, mocks.
Your final mocks should replay the most common questions, not new ones.
Rest is part of preparation; avoid cramming the night before interviews.
5-3.doneWhen: Your totals match the plan, and your last mocks went smoothly without new material.
